claims.text: High configurational entropy drives selective surface segregation of reactive constituents such as Cr, Al, or Si during high-temperature exposure.
Selective segregation of reactive constituents promotes in-situ nucleation of a continuous, adherent, multicomponent protective oxide scale.
The multicomponent protective oxide scale can self-heal during high-temperature exposure.
Sluggish diffusion is inherent in high-entropy alloys and stabilizes their protective oxide layer.
The stabilized oxide layer significantly reduces oxygen ingress relative to lower-entropy or binary alloys.
At elevated temperatures, a strong thermodynamic driving force causes reactive elements to segregate and enrich the alloy surface.
The surface-enriched elements form thermodynamically stable oxides.
The resulting oxide scale is coherent and adherent.
Continuous repair of minor oxide defects blocks further oxidation.
Under the proposed oxidation conditions, the high-entropy alloy will form a thin, continuous, well-adherent oxide layer enriched in reactive elements.
The high-entropy alloy will have a lower parabolic oxide-growth rate constant than the lower-entropy control.
Reactive-element enrichment will be detectable at the oxide-metal interface.
A lower-entropy binary or ternary alloy with similar reactive-element content will form a thicker oxide scale under identical conditions.
The lower-entropy control scale will be less adherent and more defect-prone, leading to spallation or greater oxygen ingress.
The proposed mechanism applies approximately from 800 to 1200°C in oxidizing atmospheres.
The mechanism requires reactive elements above an approximate threshold of 10 at.%.
The proposed behavior may fail at much higher temperatures, in non-oxidizing environments, or in alloys lacking sufficient reactive constituents.
Exposure at 1000°C in air for 100 hours, with time-resolved composition, morphology, kinetics, and adhesion measurements, can test the proposed mechanism against a lower-entropy control.
Failure of the high-entropy alloy to exhibit a significantly thinner and more adherent scale with greater interfacial reactive-element enrichment than the control would falsify the hypothesis.
